hypothesis: Within a species, the share of individuals showing right-handed versus left-handed (clockwise versus counter-clockwise) phyllotactic spirals is close to 50:50, as in Thompson's 224 of 467 (48.0%) right-handed.
pass_criterion: For every species with at least 30 scored individuals, compute p = proportion with clockwise (right-handed) direction. Claim supported if at least 75% of such species have p within 0.40–0.60 (a band that contains Thompson's own 0.480), and the pooled p across species is within 0.45–0.55.
fail_criterion: Claim refuted if fewer than 50% of species with n>=30 have p within 0.40–0.60, or the pooled p lies outside 0.40–0.60 (for example a consistent counter-clockwise bias).
interpretation: Thompson's 'right-handed' and 'left-handed' parastichy directions are mapped to clockwise and counter-clockwise generative-spiral direction (phyllotactic chirality). 'Nearly equally divided' is operationalised as p between 0.40 and 0.60. Caveat: Thompson's example is Norway spruce cones, and I found no cone-specific public dataset to fetch. This plan therefore tests the within-species equal-handedness generalisation on shoot apices of calathea (Goeppertia) from iNaturalist photos, which is a different organ and taxon, so it is weaker evidence for cones. Direction is counted per photographed plant, not per cone parastichy series. The landing page returned 403 to my fetch; I read the record through the figshare API instead.
